passages.t: To the saints at Philippi, with the overseers and deacons
passages.happening:
The letter opens in the usual way of the time: who it is from, who it is to, and a greeting.

“Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus, To all the saints in Christ Jesus at Philippi, together with the overseers and deacons: Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (verses 1-2).
passages.hearers:
Paul does not call himself an apostle here, as he does at the start of most of his letters. He calls himself and Timothy ‘servants’, and the Greek word means slaves. That fits the whole letter. This is a letter between friends, and its great theme is Christ, who took ‘the form of a servant’ (2:7).

‘Saints’ does not mean especially holy people. It means all believers, people set apart for God. Every member of the church in Philippi is a saint ‘in Christ Jesus’. Notice the word ‘all’. It comes again and again in this chapter: all the saints, all of you. Paul will not let the church split into parties.

Then Paul names two kinds of leaders, ‘overseers and deacons’. This is one of the earliest mentions anywhere of recognized leaders in a local church. The word for overseer, episkopos, later became the word for a bishop. But here it is plural: Philippi had a group of overseers, probably the same people other letters call elders. Deacon means servant or helper.

‘Grace and peace’ joins the usual Greek greeting, ‘grace’, with the usual Jewish one, ‘peace’. Both now come ‘from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ’. Paul names Jesus alongside the Father as the giver of God's own gifts.
passages.ot:
Paul's title ‘servant’ has a long history in Scripture. The greatest leaders of Israel were called the LORD's servants: “So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab” (Deuteronomy 34:5). It was a title of honour, because of whose servant you were.

Israel's leaders were to be chosen for their character: “select capable men from among the people—God-fearing, trustworthy men who are averse to dishonest gain” (Exodus 18:21). The New Testament's overseers and deacons were chosen the same way, as the later letters to Timothy and Titus set out.

And the blessing of peace was Israel's oldest blessing: “may the LORD lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace” (Numbers 6:26).
passages.hard:
Who were the ‘overseers and deacons’, and what do they tell us about how a church should be led?

All agree that the church in Philippi had recognized leaders, that they served the church rather than ruling it for their own gain, and that Paul writes to the whole church first and its leaders second.

Churches today read these words differently, and these notes do not choose. Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches see here the early form of an order that grew into bishops, priests and deacons, with bishops as successors of the apostles. Presbyterian and Reformed churches see overseers as elders, a group of leaders who govern together, with deacons serving the church's practical needs. Baptist and other congregational churches see pastors and deacons serving a congregation that governs its own life under Christ.

The Pastoral Letters (1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1) say more about what these leaders were to be like. What stands out in Philippians is that Paul greets the leaders almost in passing. The letter is to ‘all the saints’.
passages.asks: Paul calls himself a servant before anything else. Ask what title you are most proud of, and whether ‘servant of Christ Jesus’ comes first. And if you lead in any way, at home, at work or in a church, ask whether the people you lead would say you serve them.

passages.t: Thanks for partnership, and a prayer for love
passages.happening:
Paul thanks God for them. “I thank my God every time I remember you. In every prayer for all of you, I always pray with joy, because of your partnership in the gospel from the first day until now” (verses 3-5).

He is sure about the future: “being confident of this, that He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus” (verse 6). He holds them in his heart (verse 7), and “God is my witness how I long for all of you with the affection of Christ Jesus” (verse 8).

Then he tells them what he prays: “that your love may abound more and more in knowledge and depth of insight, so that you may be able to test and prove what is best and may be pure and blameless for the day of Christ, filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God” (verses 9-11).
passages.hearers:
‘Partnership’ translates the Greek word koinonia. It means having something in common: a shared life and a shared cause. The Philippians did not just like Paul. They took part in his work. They prayed for him. They sent money again and again (4:15-16). They sent one of their own to care for him in prison. From the day Lydia opened her home (Acts 16:15), they had been partners.

Verse 6 is a great comfort. The ‘good work’ God began in them is his work, not theirs, and God does not leave his work half done. He will finish it ‘until the day of Christ Jesus’, the day Christ returns.

The ‘affection’ of verse 8 is a strong word in Greek, splanchna, the inward parts, where people felt deep love and pity. Paul loves them with Christ's own love.

Notice what Paul prays for. Not that their troubles go away, but that their love grows. And not a love that is only feeling, but love with ‘knowledge and depth of insight’, love that thinks, that can ‘test and prove what is best’. Real love is not blind. It learns what is truly good for another person.
passages.ot:
Paul's confidence that God will finish his work echoes the psalm: “The LORD will fulfill His purpose for me. O LORD, Your loving devotion endures forever— do not abandon the works of Your hands” (Psalm 138:8).

‘The fruit of righteousness’ recalls the picture of the righteous person as a tree: “He is like a tree planted by streams of water, yielding its fruit in season” (Psalm 1:3). Jeremiah says the same of the one who trusts the LORD: “It does not worry in a year of drought, nor does it cease to produce fruit” (Jeremiah 17:8).
passages.asks: Paul thanks God every time he remembers these friends. Ask whom you could thank God for today, and whether you have told them. Ask who your partners in the gospel are. And pray Paul's prayer for someone you love: not only that their troubles end, but that their love grows wiser.

passages.happening:
Paul gives his news. “Now I want you to know, brothers, that my circumstances have actually served to advance the gospel” (verse 12). “As a result, it has become clear throughout the whole palace guard and to everyone else that I am in chains for Christ” (verse 13). And seeing him in chains has made other believers bolder: they “now dare more greatly to speak the word without fear” (verse 14).

Not everyone preaches for good reasons. “It is true that some preach Christ out of envy and rivalry, but others out of goodwill” (verse 15). Some hope to make Paul's chains harder to bear (verse 17).

Paul's answer: “What then is the issue? Just this: that in every way, whether by false motives or true, Christ is preached. And in this I rejoice” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
The Philippians must have been worried. Their founder was in prison and might be killed. Did that mean the gospel had been stopped? Paul says no, the opposite. His chains have become a sermon.

‘The whole palace guard’ translates a Latin word, praetorium. It could mean the emperor's guard in Rome, or the headquarters of a governor in a province. Either way, the soldiers who guarded Paul had come to know why he was there.

The rivals of verses 15 to 17 were believers in the city where Paul was held. They were not teaching a false gospel; Paul would never rejoice in that (see Galatians 1). Their problem was their motives. They saw Paul's absence as a chance to make a name for themselves.

Paul's response is striking. He does not defend his reputation. He does not demand loyalty. He rejoices that Christ is preached. What mattered to him was not whether people thought well of Paul, but whether they heard about Jesus.
passages.ot:
Paul's confidence that God can turn even chains to good stands in the line of Joseph, who said to the brothers who had sold him: “As for you, what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good, in order to accomplish a day like this—to preserve the lives of many people” (Genesis 50:20).

And Isaiah says God's word does its work whoever carries it: “so My word that proceeds from My mouth will not return to Me empty, but it will accomplish what I please” (Isaiah 55:11).
passages.asks: Paul cared more that Christ was preached than that he got the credit. Ask whether you are glad when someone else's work for God goes well, or only when yours does. Ask what hard circumstance in your life God might use for good. And ask whether you have ever been made bolder by someone else's courage, and whose courage yours might strengthen.

passages.t: To live is Christ, to die is gain
passages.happening:
Paul is sure that, through their prayers and the help of the Spirit, “my distress will turn out for my deliverance” (verse 19). His hope is “that now as always Christ will be exalted in my body, whether by life or by death” (verse 20).

Then the famous line: “For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (verse 21).

Paul weighs the two. Living means “fruitful labor” (verse 22). “I am torn between the two. I desire to depart and be with Christ, which is far better indeed. But it is more necessary for you that I remain in the body” (verses 23-24). So he is convinced he will stay, “for your progress and joy in the faith” (verse 25), and come to them again (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
Paul's case was not yet decided. The trial could end in his release, or in his death. He was not writing about death from a safe distance.

Verse 21 sums up his whole life in one short sentence. If he lives, his life is Christ: knowing him, serving him, making him known. If he dies, that is gain, because he will be with Christ. Either way, Christ is at the centre.

Notice how Paul decides. He does not choose by what he wants most. What he wants for himself is to be with Christ. But he chooses what others need: ‘it is more necessary for you that I remain’. The same pattern runs through the whole letter: looking to the interests of others (2:4), as Christ did.

‘Deliverance’ in verse 19 can mean rescue from prison, or the final salvation God gives. Paul may mean both: whether he is freed or not, God will vindicate him.
passages.ot:
When Paul says his distress ‘will turn out for my deliverance’, his Greek words match the old Greek translation of Job 13:16, where Job, in great suffering, trusts that God will vindicate him. The BSB, translating the Hebrew, reads, “Moreover, this will be my salvation” (Job 13:16). Like Job, Paul expects God to make things right, whatever human judges decide.

The Psalms already knew that God himself is the greatest good, in life and beyond it: “Whom have I in heaven but You? And on earth I desire no one besides You. My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever” (Psalm 73:25-26). And, “You will fill me with joy in Your presence” (Psalm 16:11).
passages.hard:
What happens when a believer dies? Does ‘to depart and be with Christ’ mean being with him at once?

All Christians confess that Christ has conquered death, that believers who die belong to him, and that the final hope is the resurrection of the body when he returns (3:20-21). Paul is sure that to depart is to be ‘with Christ’, and that this is ‘far better’.

Beyond that, as the site's note on this chapter says, Christians differ about the time between death and the resurrection. Most Christians through history have read these words to mean that believers who die go at once into Christ's presence, aware and at rest, though still waiting for the body to be raised. They point also to 2 Corinthians 5:8, ‘away from the body and at home with the Lord’, and to Jesus' words to the thief on the cross (Luke 23:43). A smaller number of Christians hold that the dead sleep, unaware, until the resurrection, so that departing and being with Christ will seem to them to happen at once. These notes do not choose. The doctrine study ‘Death and the Intermediate State’ sets out the views.

One more thing must be said plainly. Paul is not wishing to end his own life. He longs for Christ, and he chooses to stay because others need him. If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Try finishing Paul's sentence for yourself: ‘For to me, to live is …’. Ask what you would honestly put there: work, family, comfort, being liked. Ask whether death would be gain or loss by that measure. And notice how Paul chose: by what others needed. Ask who needs you to stay faithful where you are.

passages.t: Live as citizens worthy of the gospel
passages.happening:
“Nevertheless, conduct yourselves in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ” (verse 27). Whether Paul comes or not, he wants to hear that they “stand firm in one spirit, contending side by side for the faith of the gospel, without being frightened in any way by those who oppose you” (verses 27-28).

Then a surprising word: “For it has been granted to you on behalf of Christ not only to believe in Him, but also to suffer for Him” (verse 29). They are in the same struggle they saw Paul face in Philippi, and now hear he still faces (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
‘Conduct yourselves’ translates a verb that means to live as a citizen, to carry out your duties in a city. Philippi was a Roman colony whose people were proud to be Roman citizens. Paul tells them they now belong to another kingdom, and should live in a way worthy of it.

‘Contending side by side’ is a word from the sports ground: athletes who strive together as one team. The church's strength is in standing together.

The Philippians faced opposition of their own. In a city that honoured the gods and the emperor, believers who would not join in probably faced pressure from their neighbours. Paul tells them not to be frightened.

Then verse 29. Suffering for Christ is called something ‘granted’, a gift of grace, like faith itself. That does not mean suffering is good in itself. It means that to suffer for Christ's sake is to share in his life, and that the church's troubles are not a sign that God has left it. They had seen Paul and Silas beaten and jailed in their own city (Acts 16:22-24). They were walking the same road.
passages.ot:
God's people had long been told not to fear their enemies, because God was with them: “The LORD is my light and my salvation— whom shall I fear?” (Psalm 27:1). “Do not fear, for I am with you; do not be afraid, for I am your God. I will strengthen you; I will surely help you” (Isaiah 41:10).

And the Psalms say that the suffering of God's faithful people is seen and valued by him: “Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of His saints” (Psalm 116:15).
passages.asks: Paul asks believers to live as citizens of Christ's kingdom. Ask what would change if people judged that kingdom by how you live. Ask whom you stand side by side with, and whether you have left anyone to stand alone. And if you are suffering for doing what is right, hear that this is not a sign God has left you.
